opus-5.5.text:
Well, if you look at how these models work today, they essentially have two kinds of memory. There's the context window, which is a bit like working memory: very rich, very precise, but short-lived. Once the conversation is over, it's gone. And then there's the weights, which are where the model's long-term knowledge lives. But the weights get set through this enormous, slow training process, where you show the model the same kinds of information many, many times and it gradually soaks it in.

What's missing is something in between. Humans have episodic memory, where you can experience something once, a particular conversation, a particular event, and you can store it and recall it later. You don't need to see it a thousand times. That's largely what the hippocampus does in the brain. It rapidly encodes specific experiences, and then over time, maybe during sleep, some of that gets consolidated into the more general knowledge in the cortex.

Current architectures just don't have a mechanism like that. You can't simply make the context window longer and longer forever. That gets very expensive, and it isn't really the same thing anyway. And you can't just fine-tune the weights every time something happens, because gradient descent is a slow, statistical learning process that tends to blur things together or overwrite what was there before. So to get that fast, one-shot learning of specific experiences that persist, I think you need some new component in the architecture, some kind of memory system that sits alongside the existing pieces and is designed to do that job.

I don't think it's an insurmountable problem. People are working on it, and there are various ideas around. But I do think it's one of the genuine gaps between where these systems are now and something that learns from experience more like a person does.

r001.rationale: It explicitly compares the context window to working memory.

r002.rationale: It describes weights as long-term knowledge and mentions later consolidation into the cortex, but does not liken the weights themselves to cortical synapses.

r003.rationale: It contrasts rapid, one-shot storage of specific experiences with slow, repeated statistical learning of general knowledge as distinct processes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think you have to start by looking at what these models are actually doing when they appear to remember something. Right now, a language model has essentially two kinds of memory. It has the weights, which is this very slow, very diffuse form of learning that happens during training, and it has the context window, which is working memory. And that's it. There's nothing in between.

Now, humans have this very distinctive capacity where you have an experience once, a specific event in a specific place at a specific time, and you can recall it later, often for the rest of your life. You don't need to be exposed to it a thousand times. You don't rehearse it. It just gets written down, so to speak, and it's indexed in a way that lets you retrieve it when something relevant comes up. That's episodic memory, and the brain has dedicated machinery for it. The hippocampus and surrounding structures are doing something quite different from what the cortex is doing. It's fast, it's sparse, it's one-shot.

If you try to get that out of a transformer as it currently exists, you run into problems on both sides. If you try to put it into the weights, you need gradient updates, and gradient descent is fundamentally a slow, averaging process. It's designed to extract statistical regularities across enormous amounts of data, not to store a single event faithfully. Push hard enough to make one event stick and you start interfering with everything else. That's the catastrophic forgetting problem, and it's not really solved.

If you try to put it into the context window, then you're just making the window longer and longer. People sometimes say, well, with a million-token context, isn't that episodic memory? And I'd say no, not really. For one thing, it's expensive. Attention over a very long context is costly, and you're paying that cost on every step. But more fundamentally, it's not organised. It's just a long sequence that the model attends over. There's no process deciding what's worth keeping, no consolidation, no structure that reflects the fact that some things happened yesterday and some things happened a year ago and some things are important and some aren't.

So what you really want is a third system. Something that can take an experience, encode it rapidly without disturbing the core model, store it in a way that scales to a very long lifetime of experience, and then retrieve the right pieces at the right time and feed them back into the computation. People have been working on this for a long time, actually. If you go back to the Neural Turing Machine or the Differentiable Neural Computer work, that was very much about this. External memory, read and write heads, learned addressing. Retrieval augmented generation is a more pragmatic version of the same instinct, although in most implementations the retrieval isn't really learned end to end and it isn't really about the agent's own experience.

And then there's the question of what retrieval should even be driven by. In the brain it's deeply tied to context, emotion, novelty, surprise. The things you remember vividly are the things that mattered or that violated your expectations. You'd want something analogous, some signal that says this is worth storing, and that signal has to come from somewhere other than next-token prediction loss.

So my view is that this isn't something you get by scaling the current recipe. You can get a bit further with longer contexts and clever caching, and that's useful, but it's not the thing itself. The thing itself requires a component that's architecturally distinct, with different learning dynamics, operating on a different timescale. And I think that's one of the more important missing pieces if you're serious about agents that actually live in the world over long periods and learn from what happens to them.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls the context window “working memory.”

r002.rationale: It describes model weights and contrasts the hippocampus with the cortex, but does not liken the weights to synapses in the cortex.

r003.rationale: It contrasts fast, one-shot storage of specific events with slow gradient-based learning of statistical regularities, describing them as requiring different learning dynamics.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t think it necessarily requires changing the underlying transformer. But it does require changing the system around it. At the moment, a language model has what it learned during training, and then it has whatever you put into its context. If something happened in a previous conversation and it’s in neither of those places, the model has no way of remembering it.

You can put past conversations into a database and retrieve relevant pieces. That’s a useful starting point. But then you have to decide what to store, how to represent it, when to retrieve it, and how to use it. You also need to distinguish something you experienced from something somebody merely told you, and recognize when new information supersedes an old memory.

So the architectural change I have in mind is a system that can write memories as it operates and bring the right memories back into its reasoning. A longer context helps, but there’s still the question of how you manage a lifetime of experience without having to process the whole thing every time you want to make a decision.

r001.rationale: The response describes what is in a model’s context, but does not compare the context window to biological working memory.

r002.rationale: It mentions information learned during training, but does not liken model weights to cortical synapses.

r003.rationale: It discusses storing and retrieving memories, but does not distinguish rapid learning of specific information from slow learning of deep generalities as separate optimization problems.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think it necessarily requires changing the transformer itself. But it does require changing the system around it. At the moment, a language model has what it learned during training, and then it has whatever you put in its context window. Neither of those is quite episodic memory.

What you want is for the system to remember particular experiences: what happened, in what situation, what it tried, and what the outcome was. And then, when it encounters a new situation, it needs to bring back the relevant experiences without bringing back everything it’s ever seen.

You can get some of that by storing interactions in a database and retrieving them. But then you have questions like: What should you store? How should you represent it? When should you retrieve it? How does the model know whether a memory is relevant or reliable? Those decisions are part of the intelligence of the system.

So the architectural change, in that broader sense, is giving the model a persistent memory that it can write to and read from, and training it to use that effectively. Simply making the context window longer helps, but it doesn’t by itself solve the problem of learning from a lifetime of experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes the context window as something that holds supplied information, but does not compare it to biological working memory.

r002.rationale: It mentions what the model learned during training, but does not liken model weights to cortical synapses.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes training, context, and episodic memory, but does not contrast rapid learning of specific information with slow learning of deep generalities as different optimization problems.
